title: Sudama's Handful of Rice
hookLine: a poor friend hides a handful of rice from a king, and Vaisheshika names the unseen fruit of every deed
carry: adrishta: every deed bears unseen fruit
tomorrow: a mother asks her son what ends sorrow

lines: A POOR FRIEND, A HANDFUL OF RICE.
cards: In the Bhagavata Purana, a poor Brahmin, the one families know as Sudama, is told by his wife: you went to school with Krishna, and now he's king of Dvaraka. Go and see him. He has nothing to bring.

So she begs a few handfuls of flattened rice from the neighbors and ties them in a corner of his worn cloth. At the palace, Krishna runs to meet him and washes his feet. Sudama, ashamed, keeps the rice hidden.

Krishna notices anyway, pulls the bundle free and eats a handful with delight: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, he says, offered with love, I accept. Sudama walks home without asking for a thing.
Where his hut stood, he finds a palace.

teach.b: Vaisheshika has a word for what runs underneath that story: adrishta, the unseen. The Vaisheshika Sutra says the upward flaming of fire, the sideways blowing of wind, even the first motion of the atoms come from adrishta.

teach.h: EVERY DEED LEAVES PUNYA, OR ITS OPPOSITE.
teach.b: In this school, every action leaves something behind that no one can see, merit, punya, or its opposite, and that residue keeps working until it bears fruit.
This is the Hindu teaching of karma at its most physical: the deed is over, and its fruit is still on the way. Then a question. Who keeps track?
Later Nyaya-Vaisheshika thinkers, Udayana among them, argued that the unseen needs a knower to guide it, and that the knower is Ishvara, God, who brings each deed to its fruit.
Not every reader of the old Sutra sees God there; the school has room for that debate. But look at the story again.
Sudama hid his gift. Krishna saw it.

teach.h: THE FRUIT IS ON THE WAY.
teach.b: Sudama asked for nothing, and the fruit came anyway. It's one reason many Hindu families prize gupt daan, secret giving: an extra plate for a guest, a coin in the temple box, and no one told.
Punya doesn't need an audience. And today, the kindness nobody noticed isn't lost. In Hindu terms, it's already moving.

how: In the Nyaya-Vaisheshika tradition, adrishta is taught as the unseen result of past actions, and later thinkers such as Udayana argued that Ishvara guides it. Sudama's story is told at Krishna festivals, and at the Guruvayur temple in Kerala, on Kuchela Dinam, devotees offer flattened rice to Krishna in memory of him (Kuchela is his name in Malayalam tradition).

o: a temple dance that tells a story with the hands
the school where every deed leaves an unseen force
a festival lamp lit for the ancestors at dusk

p: hid a handful of flattened rice
merit a good deed leaves behind
argued that Ishvara guides the unseen

s: the Vaisheshika Sutra says even the first motion of the atoms comes from adrishta
fire rising, wind blowing sideways, the first motion of atoms and of mind: all from the unseen.
in Hindu teaching, a good deed only counts if someone sees it
adrishta is unseen by definition: a deed's fruit keeps working whether anyone noticed or not.
Sudama asked Krishna to make him rich
he never asked. he went home empty-handed and found the fruit already there.

games.q: you're Sudama at the palace, holding a few handfuls of flattened rice for a king. by the story and by Vaisheshika, what fits?
o: offer it, small as it is: a deed's fruit doesn't depend on its size or its audience.
keep it hidden: a gift that small can't count for anything.
go home: without a big gift, the visit won't matter.
games.why: Krishna took the hidden rice himself and ate it with joy. what's offered with love leaves something behind, seen or not.

practice: Sit for a couple of minutes and bring to mind one thing you did yesterday that nobody saw: a kind word, a sharp one, a promise kept or dropped.

Don't judge it; just notice that it isn't finished, that something of it is still moving. If you pray, you can offer that deed to Krishna, or the name of God you use, the way Sudama's rice was offered.
If you don't, simply hold it, and let it be seen by you.

wordCard.voice: Vaisheshika. The school of atoms and categories, where even the first motion of the world runs on adrishta, the unseen fruit of what we do.

orig.note: Sanskrit: adrishta, the unseen; in Vaisheshika, the unseen force left by actions.

carryVoice: Your line: adrishta, every deed bears unseen fruit. Sudama hid his rice, and it was seen anyway. Until tomorrow.
